guidelines.intro: Two expert bodies, read side by side. The US review grades how confident the evidence is that an agent beats placebo; the European guideline says where an agent belongs in practice, weighing side effects as well as efficacy.

essts.label: ESSTS 2022 (Europe)
essts.note: 'Not named' means the agent does not appear in the guideline's summary recommendations; it is not a recommendation against use. Tiapride, also named by ESSTS, is not marketed in the US.

takeaways: Aripiprazole is the point of agreement: moderate-confidence evidence in the US review and the preferred agent in Europe.
Haloperidol shows the gap between efficacy and tolerability: moderate-confidence evidence, yet Europe reserves it for treatment-resistant cases because of movement side effects.
Guanfacine is widely used first but rests on low-confidence evidence; both bodies tie the alpha-2 agonists most closely to patients who also have ADHD.
None of the VMAT2 inhibitors is rated or named by either body.

also.text: The AACAP practice parameter (2013) recommends a stepped, multimodal approach for children and adolescents. Its agent-by-agent positions are not shown because only secondary summaries of it could be checked.

oversight.title: Medicaid oversight of antipsychotics in children
oversight.intro: Most current Tourette medicines with the strongest evidence are antipsychotics, and state Medicaid programs apply extra controls when these are prescribed to children.

facts.text: A 50-state review found 31 state Medicaid programs required prior authorization for atypical antipsychotics in children. Only 7 applied it through age 18; most stopped at ages 5 to 7. Fifteen included peer review by a physician.

The SUPPORT Act (section 1004) required every state to run a program to monitor and manage antipsychotic use in children enrolled in Medicaid, including children in foster care, and to report on it each year.
48 states reported managing or monitoring antipsychotic use in children.
CMS's national summary reports that all states have such a program in place.

oversight.why: Oversight is now universal, so the question for any state is how its program works: which ages, which checks, and whether a prescriber review is required. Whether a new non-antipsychotic medicine falls inside or outside these programs is decided state by state.
oversight.gap: A current state-by-state record of these rules could not be obtained. CMS publishes the state answers as report documents, not as data, and the last published 50-state comparison describes 2013 to 2014. No state is shown as having or lacking a specific rule.
